title: Comps gotchas
objectives: Answer out loud: What do you do with a negative-EBITDA comp?
Answer out loud: What drives multiple compression?

blocks.title: What if a comp has negative EBITDA?
blocks.body: The EV/EBITDA multiple is meaningless (negative). Mark it "NM" (not meaningful) and exclude it from that column, or use EV/revenue.

blocks.prompt: One comp has negative EBITDA. What do you do with its EV/EBITDA?

options.text: Use it — negative multiples mean the stock is cheap
Mark it NM and exclude it, or use EV/revenue
Replace it with the industry average

blocks.explanation: A negative EV/EBITDA is meaningless. Mark it "NM" and exclude it from that column (or use EV/revenue).

blocks.title: What if one multiple is an outlier?
blocks.teaser: Investigate why — a pending acquisition, a one-time earnings hit, a data error.
blocks.body: Investigate why — a pending acquisition, a one-time earnings hit, a data error. Exclude it if it's not representative, and say so.

blocks.title: Why might multiples compress even if a company's earnings grow?
blocks.teaser: Rising interest rates increase discount rates, so investors pay less per dollar of earnings.
blocks.body: Rising interest rates increase discount rates, so investors pay less per dollar of earnings. Sector sentiment and growth slowdowns also compress multiples.

blocks.title: Can you use a comp from a different country?
blocks.teaser: Yes, but adjust for accounting differences (leases under IFRS — see 1.7), tax rates, and country risk.
blocks.body: Yes, but adjust for accounting differences (leases under IFRS — see 1.7), tax rates, and country risk. Market multiples also differ by region.
